Dear Reviewer jFWp:

Thank you for your constructive suggestions for our previous draft. We have revised the paper completely. And we hope these modifications can well solve your concerns and you can reconsider the rating with our newest version.

We mainly changed the paper in the following aspects, corresponding to your concerns.
- Adding more related works. We cited earlier related works, including [1]. This work [1] is an early attempt to utilize the infrastructure data to enhance autonomous driving ability. However, this work mainly focuses on control, and they directly transmit the raw images to vehicles. This transmission requires huge transmission costs, which is one of the main challenges in solving the vehicle-infrastructure cooperative perception. And our work focuses on transmitting lightweight data to improve the detection performance with our proposed FFNet.
- Adding more experiment details and releasing the code to improve the confidence in reproducibility. We updated the FFNet overview in Figure 2 to remove confusion for readers. We added more network settings in Appendix and more training details in Section 3.3. Besides, **we release the code in an anonymous Github. The code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/FFNet-VIC3D-ICLR3614.**
- Reorganizing and rewriting the experiment parts. To make the experiment better illustrate the effectiveness of our FFNet, we reorganized the experiment section and extracted some clear points to explain the advantages of FFNet. Besides, we moved the relatively unimportant ablation study experiment to Appendix.
- Adding more 3D detection methods in experiments. We added more 3D detection methods like PointPillars[2] on DAIR-V2X. And our FFNet still outperforms these methods. Besides, to demonstrate that infrastructure data can significantly improve the detection upper bound, we provide some videos at the anonymous link:https://drive.google.com/file/d/15obrfwke32YbO2gNPZ0aQiT6gETuauK2/view?usp=sharing. This link contains three videos: vehicle-view detection video, infra-view detection video, and cooperative-view detection video. In the vehicle-view detection video, there is a car occluded by other obstacles and cannot be seen in the ego-vehicle view in some frames. And it cannot be detected only using ego-vehicle data. But this occluded car can be seen and detected from infra-view data as infra-view detection video shows. So, we can detect this occlude car by utilizing both infra data and ego-vehicle data, as the cooperative-view detection video shows.
- Clarifying the misunderstanding about “N”. In the previous draft, we used N historical and current infrastructure frames to generate feature flow. "N=1" means we used two infrastructure frames to generate the feature flow. To avoid misunderstanding, we regarded the current infrastructure frame as the historical infrastructure frame and claimed N=2 in the newest version.
- Added more motivation analysis for the feature flow and cosine similarity loss.
- Added more explanation for the notations and fixed the typo errors.

Besides, we explain why we only choose the DAIR-V2X [2] as our experimental dataset. Many 3D object detection datasets exist in autonomous driving, such as Kitti [4] and nuScenes [5]. However, they are all captured by a single vehicle and unsuitable for testing the cooperative perception methods. There are also some V2V datasets, such as V2X-sim [6]. However, these datasets are from the simulator and mainly focus on V2V cases. In comparison, DAIR-V2X is the only large-scale real-world V2X dataset. So, this dataset is more suitable for testing our method.

  A: We cited earlier related works in the newest version, including [1]. These related works have also done great jobs in cooperative autonomous driving. However, they directly transmit the raw data, like raw images, to vehicles. This transmission requires huge transmission costs, which is one of the main challenges in solving the vehicle-infrastructure cooperative perception. In comparison, our work focuses on practical cooperative perception. We propose two main challenges in cooperative perception: limited communication bandwidth and temporal asynchrony. For this purpose, we present the FFNet framework to solve this cooperative perception. 

**Explaining the difference between FFNet and other related works**

Q: "While the idea and the approach is known (in the past the idea of using data from another source is already used in many applications), its application on 3D object detection might be interesting. "

A: First, we focus on 3D detection, a vital perception task in autonomous driving. In comparison, some earlier related works focus on directly improving the controlling module. One of the most significant advantages of infrastructure information is to provide extra complementary information for perception. Secondly, we focus on the practical cooperative perception, considering the limited communication bandwidth and transmitting compressed intermediate data instead of the raw data. Thirdly, we propose a feature flow prediction module for the temporal asynchrony problem mainly caused by latency. Our FFNet can effectively solve the asynchrony problem with limited communication bandwidth and computational resources on vehicle-infrastructure devices. Fourthly, FFNet training requires much less labeled data and annotation costs. With the frame pairs sampled from infrastructure video frames, we use self-supervised learning to learn the temporal information and train the feature flow generator. Dear Reviewer FYpB:

Thanks for your valuable suggestions. We will respond to your concerns in the following aspects.

**Extending the methods on more sensors**

Our feature flow prediction module is general, and our FFNet is a general framework for cooperative perception. Firstly, our FFNet is suitable for different sensors. For example, we can use a feature flow generator to generate the feature flow from the image features and the feature flow from the multimodal features of images and point clouds. Here, the Cameras capture the images, and the LiDAR captures the point clouds. Secondly, our FFNet is suitable for more agents’ cooperative perceptions. Consider the N-M cooperative perception task of broadcasting sensor data from N infrastructure agents to M self-driving vehicles. For this N-M cooperative perception task, we can generate the feature flow for each infrastructure agent and then predict the features with the feature flow received from infrastructure agents to align the timestamp. We think it is better to claim the contributions when we conduct these experiments in the future.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This work targets the vehicle-infrastructure cooperative 3D detection (VIC3D) task.
In this task there are two major challenges - (1) limited communication bandwidth and (2) asynchronous observations.  
To tackle this problem, they present a pipeline called Feature Flow Network (FFNet).
Their pipeline sends compressed mid-level features and predicted flow from the infrastructure side and decompress these on the vehicle side (reducing transmission costs).
These are then used to predict time-aligned features (addressing the asynchronous issue), which are then is fused with the vehicle's feature to ultimately perform 3D object detection.  
Their proposed pipeline achieves state-of-the-art performance on the DAIR-V2X dataset (cooperative driving detection dataset).

Dear Reviewer BTWR:

Thanks for your valuable suggestions. We will respond to your concerns in the following aspects.

**Improving the writing quality**

In our newest draft, we made the following changes to your concerns.
- We moved the related work to the main paper and some ablation study experiments to Appendix. 
- We described the DiscoNet and V2VNet in Appendix.
- We rewrote the original 2.2 and 2.3 to make the expression clearer.
- We updated the FFNet overview in Figure 2 to clarify the first-order derivative generator. (Yes, we use another network to generate the first-order derivative.)
- We updated the original busy Figure 3 and fixed typo errors.
- We updated the Original Table 1 to make the claims clearer. The original bold numbers were used to demonstrate the effect of FFNet.

Apart from the above changes, we also thoroughly revised the previous draft. 

**Explaining the importance of less transmission cost**

As Tab. 1 in the paper shows, the average amount of the infrastructure point cloud in DAIR-V2X is 1.4Mb. Suppose only one self-driving vehicle on the road needs to receive the infrastructure data. Naive early fusion will consume 14Mb/s communication bandwidth if we transmit the raw point clouds at 10HZ. When more self-driving vehicles here need to receive infrastructure data (e.g., 100 self-driving vehicles), there will need massive communication bandwidth of up to 1,400 Mb/s. This bandwidth consumption will cause severe communication congestion and is unaffordable for the complex traffic scene. So, reducing the transmission cost is vital in vehicle-infrastructure cooperative autonomous driving. Although our FFNet only requires 1/10 of the transmission cost compared to early fusion, we still hope to reduce the bandwidth in future research further to meet the needs of real autonomous driving scenarios.

**Adding a vanilla 3D detection baseline**

We add a non-fusion baseline by ignoring infrastructure observations completely and using PointPillars [1], the classical 3D detection method in autonomous driving, to solve the VIC3D detection on the DAIR-V2X dataset [2]. We also provide experimental results in Table 1 in the paper. Our FFNet outperforms the non-fusion method, demonstrating that infrastructure data can effectively improve detection performance.

| Model   | Fusion Type        | 3D-mAP (IoU=0.5) | BEV-mAP (IoU=0.5) |
| ----------- | ----------- | ----------- | ----------- |
| PointPillars [1] |  Non-Fusion | 48.06 | 52.24 |
| FFNet | Middle Fusion | 55.37 |63.20 |

But this occluded car can be seen and detected from infra-view data as infra-view detection video shows. So, we can detect this occlude car by utilizing both infra data and ego-vehicle data, as the cooperative-view detection video shows. This result demonstrates that infra data can significantly improve the detection upper bound. **The videos are available at the anonymous link :

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper addresses the problem of fusing fixed infrastructure sensing with on-vehicle sensing to provide complementary data for 3d object detection in autonomous-driving use-cases. They tackle the problem of asynchronicity between the two data sources by predicting image features for the infra-side images and forwarding that prediction to the vehicle model which can then account for latency incurred between infra sensors and the vehicle sensors.  A nice feature of this method is that the predictive model can be trained in a self-supervised fashion using historical video frames. This method also requires low bandwidth connection between infra and vehicles due to the ability to compress and decompress and still align image features in time.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The strengths of this paper are as follows:
* Presents a somewhat practical method to fuse infra and on-vehicle sensing to account for latency.
* Method has low bandwidth requirements using data compression since latency incurred due to compressing/uncompressing can be compensated for by the technique. 

Weaknesses:
* This approach has limited novelty (see below for more details)
* This approach assumes that both infra and vehicles operate on the same clock so that the infra-vehicle lag can be calculated.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
This is a fairly clear paper and I think would be reproducible based on the description.  The one exception on clarity is during the discussion of empirical results.  The empirical results perform a comparison where the feature flow is calculated on-vehicle rather than on infra.  I don't understand why this would result in different results.  The paper would be improved if the authors could explain that point in more detail.   I can see that there are certain practical advantages to performing this extra calculation on the infra side where power and compute may be higher, but I don't see why the end-result would be affected by changing where this computation is performed.  

Using prediction to deal with latency is a standard technique in high-performance applications such as VR and AR rendering.  The present application differs in that both the latencies present are orders of magnitude higher but the alignment tolerance is order of magnitude lower.  So there is a question of novelty of this method, but personally I find that the application is different enough.

One flaw that I see in the practicality of the method is that this method assumes that the infra and vehicle are operating with syncronized clocks (needed to calculate what latency the on-vehicle model needs to assume).  I'm not sure how practical that assumption is.  The paper would benefit from a discussion on whether that is really an assumption and how realistic it is.  If it's not an assumption of the method, then please describe how the vehicle model can determine what the latency is.
content.summary_of_the_review: Interesting unsupervised method to handle latency between infra and on-vehicle sensing for fusing data across different sensors. The novelty is marginal and the use-case is fairly narrow, but autonomous driving is an important field and this could still be quite impactful.

content.comment:
Dear Reviewer yCnj:

Thank you for your valuable suggestions. We will respond to your concerns in the following three aspects.

**Explaining why calculating feature flow on infra performs better than on-vehicle**

Calculating feature flow on infra uses all the raw point clouds as inputs. This will give us more valuable information than using compressed features as inputs. To better illustrate the comparison, we also provide the implementation framework for calculating the feature flow on-vehicle in Figure 5 in Appendix.

**Adding more related works and analyses about communication latency**

Communication latency is a common problem in many areas, such as industry IoT [1], parallel computing [2], VR [3], and VR [4]. Communication latency is also one of the challenges in vehicle-infrastructure autonomous driving. However, the main contribution of this paper focuses on utilizing the infrastructure data for better 3D object detection with a novel feature flow prediction method to solve the latency challenge under limited transmission cost. Autonomous driving is a promising and vital field, and we hope to get more inspiration from other research areas to improve autonomous driving in the future. 

**Explaining the latency calculation**

Firstly, each data frame has a timestamp aligned with the sensor capturing. At the same time, each sensor has gotten the GPS timing, and the timestamp of the data frame is under the same time system. So, we can diff the timestamps between the two-side data. Secondly, the infra and vehicle sensors have different sensor initializations and are not synchronized clocks. We mainly focus on latency since the temporal asynchrony caused by the sensor asynchrony clocks is much smaller than the latency. Thirdly, our method can also address the temporal asynchrony caused by the different sensor initialization. We calculate the time difference between infra data and vehicle data for feature prediction. And the time difference is composed of the communication latency and different sensor sampling.

content.title: More explanations about the difference between FFNet and other latency prediction research
content.comment:
Dear Reviewer yCnj:

We will further explain how the feature flow prediction in our FFNet differs from the latency prediction for other traditional applications such as VR and AR rendering [1, 2].

- **The scenarios and latency magnitudes are different.** VR and AR rendering are mainly short-distance communication. However, vehicle-infrastructure cooperative 3D (VIC3D) object detection requires long-distance communication to transmit the information from infrastructure to vehicle, up to a hundred meters. This long-distance communication will cause more severe latency problems than VR and AR. 

- **The objective of latency prediction is different.** VR and AR rendering mainly use prediction to alleviate the feeling of visual latency. So they focus on predicting the complete data. In comparison, we fuse the infrastructure and ego-vehicle data to improve the perception ability. **Cooperative perception requires transmitting valuable information for fusion and perception complementary while reducing the transmission cost to reduce the communication bandwidth requirement.** For this purpose, we propose sending the feature flow, the intermediate data extracted from the raw point clouds, which can be used for predicting the future valuable feature instead of the complete data.

- **The prediction approach is different.** Most prediction approaches use historically received data to predict future data. **Conversely, we propose a new transmission form, feature flow, with the prediction attribute before transmitting.** This lightweight intermediate data with prediction attribute is suitable for solving the vehicle-infrastructure cooperative perception task. We hope this new transmission form can also have inspiration for other research areas.

content.title: General Response
content.comment:
Dear all reviewers:

We sincerely appreciate the reviewers for your time and efforts on the review. We first address the common concerns and then respond to each reviewer separately. We hope our response can clarify the existing doubts and address the problems.

**Improving the writing quality (R1/R2/R4)**

We integrated the reviewers' suggestions and revised the paper thoroughly to make the paper clearer. We mainly change the paper in the following aspects:
- Reorganized the related work part and added more associated references. We especially moved the related work from the Appendix to the main paper.
- Added more motivation analysis for the feature flow and cosine similarity loss.
- Made the FFNET implementation clearer. We significantly updated figure 1 of the FFNET overview and added more implementation details in Appendix. We also provided the training and inference code of FFNET.
- Reorganized the experiment part and made claim points clearer.
- Added more experiments like no fusion methods.
- Added more explanation for the notations and fixed the typo errors.

**Adding a vanilla 3D detection baseline. (R2/R4)**

We added a vanilla 3D detection baseline in Table 1. We see that our FFNet outperforms the single-vehicle method. **We made a video demo illustrating how infrastructure data improves detection performance.** The video demo is available at the anonymous link: https://drive.google.com/file/d/15obrfwke32YbO2gNPZ0aQiT6gETuauK2/view?usp=sharing.

**Releasing the code to improve confidence in reproducibility. (R4)**

We provided the full training and inference code for FFNET as well as the trained checkpoints in anonymous GitHub to ease the reproducible concerns. The code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/FFNet-VIC3D-ICLR3614.

content.title: Paper Decision
content.metareview:_summary,_strengths_and_weakn:
# Summary
This paper focus on the vehicle-infrastructure cooperative 3D detection (VIC3D) task by  fusing fixed infrastructure sensing with on-vehicle sensing to provide complementary data for 3d object detection in autonomous-driving use-cases. In this task there are two major challenges - (1) limited communication bandwidth and (2) asynchronous observations. The authors propose Feature Flow Network (FFNet) to deal with the problem of temporal asynchrony caused by different sensor initialization and latency. Their pipeline sends compressed mid-level features and predicted flow from the infrastructure side and decompress these on the vehicle side (reducing transmission costs). These are then used to predict time-aligned features (addressing the asynchronous issue), which are then is fused with the vehicle's feature to ultimately perform 3D object detection. Their proposed pipeline achieves state-of-the-art performance on the DAIR-V2X dataset (cooperative driving detection dataset).
# Strengths:
- Presents a somewhat practical method to fuse infra and on-vehicle sensing to account for latency.
- Method has low bandwidth requirements using data compression since latency incurred due to compressing/uncompressing can be compensated for by the technique.
- Method is relatively well motivated and easy to understand
- Simple and effective approach to a newer real-world task VIC3D
- The feature flow prediction concept is very interesting and has many advantages for this application.
# Weaknesses:
- This approach has limited novelty
- This approach assumes that both infra and vehicles operate on the same clock so that the infra-vehicle lag can be calculated.
- Writing needs some polish -  reviewers had some issues reading and understanding what the authors were trying to convey
- Results include comparison for various fusion methods, but how well do vanilla 3D detection baselines perform on this dataset? i.e. ignore infrastructure observations completely.
- The principle of feature flow is presented here for a Lidar but it can be generalized, to my point of view, to many other sensors (on infrastructure or embedded). Would it be interesting to describe the contribution in a more general context with more than two sensors and more than two hosts?
- Some details of the proposed architecture (given in Figure 2) are not provided. Furthermore, Figure 2 states that it is for "inference". That creates the confusion of how the training architecture would differ from the given figure. That should be clarified.
- The experiments and experimental results are somewhat limited and not well explained. An additional dataset could be used. More baseline algorithms could be used for comparison. 
- Some of the earlier relevant work is not cited. For example, even if its application is not object detection, the work by Valiente, Rodolfo, et al. with title: "Controlling steering angle for cooperative self-driving vehicles utilizing CNN and LSTM-based deep networks" is an early work which structured the problem of sharing image data in v2v environments.
content.justification_for_why_not_higher_score: First of all, I would like to apologize the lack of discussion among reviewers and authors because the author provided an extensive author feedback. However, the paper has been changed significantly; hence the paper should be reviewed again addressing the concerns and highlighting the contributions to avoid the practical contributions.
